youtubeTitle: The Gospel and Soul Health Session 25 - Dr Bruce Wauchope
topic: Abiding and the new command: 'let me love you'
summary: Bruce continues his theme of Christ as the 'rod of iron' and cornerstone, rising from within to break our clay structures so we can receive love. The apostles' suffering, he argues, is not a failure of faith but the breaking of earthen vessels so that Christ's life can be seen, which contradicts prosperity teaching. Abiding means remaining: staying present with Christ in our flesh, darkness and pain rather than climbing up or dissociating. Jesus' new commandment is not the Mosaic 'love God, love neighbour' but first 'let me love you', and loving others flows from that, including in the parts of ourselves we reject. He closes by saying that because Christ is in everyone, we cannot treat anyone as 'other', and that healing and miracles come inside-out through unveiling, not through power or technique.
keyPoints: The 'rod of iron' is the same as the cornerstone laid in Zion (Isaiah 28:16): Christ rising from within breaks our structures so that we learn to receive love. We either fall on the stone and are broken, or it falls on us and grinds us to powder.

Nothing separates us from the love of Christ (Romans 8), yet the apostles' lives were 'thrown under the bus': beatings, shipwreck, hunger. That is incompatible with a prosperity or 'right words' gospel.

Their suffering was not a sign that 'Dad is bad'. God was breaking their clay vessels so that the treasure of Christ within could be seen: 'struck down but not destroyed', with death at work in them but not winning.
Abiding means remaining. You do not climb up to God, run out, dissociate or disappear; you stay down with Christ in you, including in your flesh, darkness and pain.
The Spirit bears witness that we are already in Christ and Christ in us (John 14:20); this is a union we cannot forge and cannot undo.
'Love God and love your neighbour' summarises the Mosaic law, which we cannot do. What the law could not do, God did by sending His Son in the likeness of sinful flesh.
Jesus' new commandment, 'love one another as I have loved you', puts 'as I have loved you' first. In effect it says, 'Let me love you,' and from that you love others. There is no other first step.
'Let me love you' is simple and terribly hard, because it means letting Christ love us in our pain and rubbish and being present with ourselves there.

For parts of ourselves we dislike, met through emotion, we 'put our arms around' them and pray for the Spirit to open that part's eyes to the love already present. The process is fractal: scales fall at every level.

Miracles restore normality, and they happen irregularly. The answer is not 'occultic Christianity', using Jesus' name or blood as technique. It is receiving love and doing only what the Father and Jesus are doing: inside-out unveiling, not impartation from a 'big man'.

Christ is in everyone, believers and unbelievers alike (2 Corinthians 5:14-16). So we can no longer regard anyone according to the flesh, and gossip, condemnation, violence and making people 'other' lose any justification. This grounds human rights.
God works bottom-up: through weak, incomplete human beings the manifold wisdom of God is made known to principalities and powers (Ephesians 3:10).

keyTerms.definition: Christ rising from within us, breaking our false structures from the inside out and the bottom up so that we can receive love.
Our fragile human structures, which God allows to be broken so that the treasure of Christ's life becomes visible.
Remaining: staying present with Christ in yourself, including your pain and darkness, rather than escaping upward or dissociating.
'Love one another as I have loved you', read as 'Let me love you' first, with love for others flowing from it.
The same unveiling, scales falling and eyes opening, repeated at every level and in every part of the self.
Healing as the restoration of normality through the unveiling of Christ in a person, not through spiritual technique or a powerful leader.
The community of believers, not an institution, through which God's wisdom is shown to the powers.

quotes: When you abide you remain. You don't climb out to climb up to God.
A new commandment I give you: let Me love you.
This is really, really simple and terribly, terribly hard.
When you meet a part of yourself that you don't like, go and put your arms around it.

caseStudy.title: The tireless volunteer
caseStudy.scenario: Daniel, 52, runs three church ministries and is admired for serving others. Privately he feels contempt for his own neediness and keeps busy so that he never sits still with the grief of his divorce. When a friend suggests he take a break, he feels panicky and guilty. He reads 'love your neighbour' as a command he must keep fulfilling.
caseStudy.analysis: Daniel is living by the Mosaic summary, 'love God, love neighbour', as a law to perform, while skipping the first step of the new command: 'let Me love you'. His busyness works as a way of 'running out' instead of abiding with Christ in his pain. The part of him he despises, his neediness, has not been embraced, so his love for others is costly and driven rather than an overflow.
pathway: Read John 13:34 slowly and notice that 'as I have loved you' comes first.
Set aside short daily times to stay present with his grief, trusting that Christ is in it with him.
When contempt for his neediness rises, 'put his arms around' that part and pray for the Spirit to open its eyes to the Father's love.
Step back from one ministry for a season so that he is serving from overflow, not drive.
See a counsellor or grief-support group to process the divorce, with professional help if low mood persists.

practices.name: Staying down
practices.how: When a painful feeling comes, set a five-minute timer and remain with it instead of distracting yourself, praying 'Jesus, You are here in this with me.'

practices.name: Embracing an unloved part
practices.how: Name one part of yourself you dislike, such as 'the anxious part' or 'the angry part'. Imagine putting your arms around it and pray: 'Holy Spirit, open the eyes of this part to know the Father's love already here.'

practices.name: Seeing Christ in the other
practices.how: Before speaking about someone you find difficult, pause and remind yourself that Christ is in them, then choose words that fit that.

reflection: Where do I tend to 'run out' or 'climb up' rather than abide with Christ in my pain?
Which parts of me am I willing to let God love, and which do I keep behind walls?
How would my view of a person I struggle with change if I really believed Christ is in them?

quiz.q: How does Bruce interpret the 'new commandment' of John 13:34?
options: Love God and love your neighbour
Obey the Ten Commandments more carefully
Let Me love you, then love others from that love
Serve others until you feel worthy of love
quiz.explain: 'As I have loved you' comes first, so receiving Christ's love is step one.

quiz.q: What does 'abiding' mean in this session?
options: Climbing up spiritually to reach God
Remaining present with Christ in yourself, including your pain
quiz.explain: Abiding means remaining, not running out, dissociating or climbing up.

quiz.q: Why does Bruce say Christ being in everyone grounds human rights?
options: Because we can no longer treat anyone as 'other' or regard them according to the flesh
Because everyone is already a believer
Because governments are ordained by God
quiz.explain: Christ in all removes any justification for condemning or harming people as outsiders.
